sentences.text: Don Aurelio brought out a very old leather-bound book from a shelf.
He opened it.
It was written in Italian.
He said, "This is Constanzi's own workshop record.
Each violin he made, he wrote down.
Where it went.
Who took it.
The measurements.
Everything.
I have this book because my father tracked it down in Cremona in 1970.
It is one of the few Constanzi workshop books that still exist." He turned to a specific page.
"Look.
Here.
Five violins delivered to a merchant in Genoa named Ravello.
The merchant paid for all five in one payment.
He was going to take them to Naples and sell them to a musical family who had commissioned them for a private quintet — one violin for each of five children."
"But the fifth," Renata said.
"What happened to the fifth." Don Aurelio shook his head slowly.
"That is what nobody knows.
The merchant did make it to Naples.
Records show he delivered five violins.
But the family who received them only kept four.
Nobody knows why.
Maybe one child did not want to play.
Maybe the fifth was damaged in transit.
Maybe it was stolen along the way and replaced with something else.
Whatever happened, the fifth Constanzi does not appear in any record after 1801.
It vanished.
My father spent thirty years looking for it.
He never found it.
He died in 2015 not knowing what happened to it."
Renata looked at the four on the wall.
Then at Don Aurelio.
"But — you said your father tracked down four of them.
Wouldn't the fifth have — surfaced somewhere.
It has been two hundred years." "Yes," said Don Aurelio.
"That is what he thought too.
That eventually it would appear at an auction, or in an old estate somewhere, and he would find it.
But it never has.
That is very strange.
A Constanzi is a valuable violin — even a small one.
If someone had it and knew what it was, they would sell it.
They would insure it.
Something.
But there has been no trace of it in two hundred years.
That means either it was destroyed — burned, lost at sea, broken — or it is somewhere where its owner does not know what it is.
Where it is being used as a normal violin.
That is what my father believed, at the end of his life.
That somewhere, someone is playing the fifth Constanzi and does not know."
"How would you know if you saw it," said Renata.
Don Aurelio thought about this.
"You would know two ways.
First — you would look at it.
It has the exact same shape as the four on the wall.
Same curls, same fingerboard, same varnish color.
Constanzi signed his violins with a specific mark inside — a small C inside a small circle, painted on the label.
If a violin has that mark, and it looks like these four, it is the fifth.
Second — you would listen.
Constanzi violins have a very particular voice.
A specific tone.
Even to an untrained ear, if you know what these four sound like, and you hear the fifth, you would know it was one of theirs."
Renata was quiet for a long time.
Then she said, "Can I hear one of them." Don Aurelio was surprised.
But he nodded.
He took one of the four down — the one that had belonged to Bernardo Molina — and he handed her a bow.
"Play something you know," he said.
"Anything.
So you hear how it sounds in your own hands." Renata put the violin under her chin.
She was very careful.
She was afraid to move too much.
She played the first few bars of a piece she had been working on — a small piece by Bach.
The sound was — she had no words for it.
Her school violin was a decent instrument.
She had thought it sounded fine.
This did not sound fine.
This sounded like a completely different thing.
It sounded like the note was already alive before she played it.
It sounded warm.
Golden.
Full.
She stopped after only a few notes because she was almost afraid to keep going.
She handed the violin back to Don Aurelio very carefully.
Don Aurelio said, "Yes.
That is what a Constanzi sounds like.
Now if you hear that sound coming from a violin you did not expect it from — that is the fifth.
That is how you would know."
Renata went home that evening on the subway with her school violin in its case, and she thought about the fifth violin the whole way.
Somewhere in the world, someone was playing it.
Maybe as an ordinary violin.
Maybe not even a violin anymore — maybe it was in an attic, or a museum in a small town, or a private collection where nobody had told anyone about it.
Two hundred years.
It could be anywhere.
It could be in Buenos Aires.
It could be in her neighborhood.
That night she could not sleep.
She had a strange feeling.
She got out her school notebook and she started writing things down.
What she knew about the violin.
What it looked like.
What the mark inside said.
Where it had last been seen — a merchant's shop in Naples in 1801.
Where it might have gone.
Ships from Naples went all over the world.
Some of them came to Buenos Aires.
Many did.
In the 1800s.
There had been a huge wave of Italian immigration to Argentina.
Whole families had come, bringing their belongings, their furniture, their instruments.
What if the fifth Constanzi had come to Argentina and had been in the same country the whole time?
On Friday she went back to pick up her violin.
She brought her notebook.
She said, when she paid for the repair — Don Aurelio waved off the money, as her teacher had said he would — she said, "Don Aurelio.
Can I tell you something.
I want to help you find the fifth violin." He looked at her for a long moment.
He did not laugh.
He said, "Renata.
My father looked for thirty years.
He was a professional.
He knew everyone in the field.
He never found it.
It is not — this is not a project for one afternoon.
Or for a schoolgirl."
"I know," said Renata.
"But — I want to try.
Because — because I heard how it sounds.
And I do not want to be a person who does not try to find something like that.
Even if it takes me my whole life." Don Aurelio was silent.
Then he said, softly, "Very well.
If you are serious.
I will tell you everything I know.
Sit down.
Take out your notebook." And he began to talk.
He talked for an hour.
About what his father had tried.
About which routes ships had taken from Naples in the early 1800s.
About Italian immigrants in Argentina and what they had brought with them.
About specific old families in Buenos Aires who had been musical.
Renata wrote it all down.
